articles.title: Read a job ad like an employer

body.support:
Most jobs start with an ad. Real ads are on job sites like **SEEK**, **Indeed** and the government’s **Workforce Australia**. Some are on a business’s own website, or in a shop window.

Read every ad for four things.

1. **The job.** What is it? Is it casual or part-time? What hours? What pay? Where?
2. **Must-haves.** “Essential” means you must have it. “Desirable” means it’s nice to have.
3. **Documents.** What do they want? Usually a **resume**. Maybe a **cover letter** (a short letter or email). Some jobs need a check. To work with kids, you need a **Working with Children Check**.
4. **How and when.** How do you apply? What is the **closing date**?
.
**Red flags** for fake jobs:
- They ask you to pay to start.
- The pay is huge for easy work.
- They only talk on WhatsApp or Telegram.
- They want your bank details before you meet.
body.core:
Most jobs start with an ad. Real ones are on job sites such as **SEEK** and **Indeed**, the government’s **Workforce Australia**, a company’s own careers page, or a sign in a shop window. Read every ad for four things.

1. **The job.** What’s the title? Is it **casual** (hours change each week), **part-time** or full-time? What hours or **availability** do they need? What’s the pay, and where is it?
2. **Must-haves.** Ads often split requirements into **essential** (you must have it) and **desirable** (it helps, but it’s not a deal-breaker). Don’t be scared off by a desirable you don’t have.
3. **Documents and checks.** Most ads want a **resume**. Many want a **cover letter** or email saying why you want the job. Some jobs need checks or cards: a **Working with Children Check** to work with kids in Victoria, a driver licence for delivery work, or a **White Card** (construction induction) to work on a building site. List these early, because some take time to get.
4. **How and when.** How do you apply: online, by email, in person? What’s the **closing date**?
.
Then check it’s real. **Red flags** for job scams:
- you have to pay for a “starter kit”, training or equipment.
- the pay is huge for very easy work.
- they only talk on WhatsApp or Telegram.
- they want your bank details or ID before you’ve even had an interview.
- there’s no real business name you can look up.
body.extend:
Most jobs start with an ad, and every ad is a carefully constructed text. You’ll find genuine ones on job boards such as **SEEK** and **Indeed**, the government’s **Workforce Australia**, employers’ own careers pages, and local noticeboards. Read each one for four things.

1. **The job.** Title, employment type (**casual**, **part-time**, full-time), hours or **availability**, pay (sometimes called **remuneration**) and location.
2. **Selection criteria.** Many ads separate **essential** requirements from **desirable** ones. Essential criteria are gatekeepers; desirable ones are tie-breakers, so apply anyway if you meet the essentials.
3. **Documents and checks.** Identify exactly what the application requires: a **resume**, a **cover letter**, availability, referees, and any mandatory checks or tickets, such as a **Working with Children Check** for child-related work in Victoria, a driver licence, or a **White Card** for construction sites. Some take weeks, so plan ahead.
4. **Process and timing.** The method of application and the **closing date**.
.
Finally, evaluate whether the ad is genuine. Job scams have grown quickly. **Red flags** include:
- an upfront payment for kits, training or equipment.
- unrealistic pay for minimal effort.
- contact only through encrypted chat apps.
- requests for bank details or identity documents before any interview.
- no verifiable business name or ABN.

caseStudies.title: The job that wasn’t

body.support:
In 2023, Australians made almost **5,000** reports about job scams to Scamwatch.

They lost about **$24 million**. That was more than double the year before.

Many of the people hit were **young**. Lots were students looking for part-time work.

The fake jobs often came through social media or WhatsApp. They promised easy money for simple tasks, like rating products online.

Then people were asked to pay money to “unlock” their earnings. The money was gone.
body.core:
In 2023, Scamwatch received almost **5,000** reports about job scams. People lost about **$24 million**, more than double the year before. Job scams were one of the fastest-growing kinds of scam in Australia.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said younger Australians were hit especially hard, including **students looking for part-time work**.

The pattern was often the same. A message arrives on social media or WhatsApp. It offers easy money for simple online tasks, like rating products. At first, small payments come through. Then the victim is told to pay money to unlock bigger earnings. That money is never seen again.

In 2024, the government’s National Anti-Scam Centre set up a special team to fight job scams.
body.extend:
In 2023, Scamwatch received almost **5,000** reports of job scams. Reported losses were about **$24 million**, more than double the year before. That made job scams one of the fastest-growing scam types in Australia.

The ACCC reported that younger Australians were hit harder than others, especially **students looking for part-time work**. So were people from migrant and non-English-speaking backgrounds.

Many followed the same script. A stranger makes contact through social media or a chat app. They offer well-paid, flexible work doing simple online “tasks”. Small early payments build trust. Then the victim must pay in their own money to “unlock” bigger earnings, which never arrive.

In 2024, the National Anti-Scam Centre set up a special team with banks and online platforms to fight job scams. Still, the best defence is a careful reader. An ad that skips the normal parts of a real job, like a business you can check, clear duties and a proper way to apply, deserves suspicion.

model.text:
**Job:** Casual sales assistant at a sports store, Shepparton. Found on SEEK.

**The job:** Casual. Thursday nights and Saturdays. Award rates.

**Must-haves:** friendly, reliable, available Saturdays.
**Nice to have:** knows about running shoes.

**Documents:** resume, plus a short email saying why I want the job and when I can work.

**How + when:** apply on SEEK by 30 May.

**Real?** Yes. It’s a store I can visit. There’s no fee, and they want a normal application.

**Fit:** Good. I play footy and know shoes. I need to update my resume first.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** $900 liking posts — red flag; supermarket via careers page — real; $150 starter kit — red flag; swim instructor with WWCC — real; bank details before interview — red flag; apprentice carpenter with White Card — real.

**Annotation:** 1 type, hours and pay; 2 duties; 3 essential criteria; 4 desirable; 5 documents and how to apply (resume + availability); 6 closing date.

**Case study:** young people, especially students seeking part-time work; contact via social media or WhatsApp, easy tasks, small early payments, then pay to unlock earnings, money lost; check the business is real, never pay to start, never send bank or ID details first.

realityCheck: **Local jobs vary hugely.** In small towns, students may find few online ads. Count shop-window, council and Facebook community ads (checked for red flags).
**Some students are under 15 or can’t work yet.** Let them hunt for jobs they could do “within a year”, or work experience.
**Students may click on scam ads.** Remind them not to reply to or contact any ad during class.
**Pay rates are confusing.** If students ask what “award rates” means, point them to the Fair Work Pay Calculator rather than guessing.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students like seeing real jobs nearby, and some apply straight after.
